Frontiers
FRUN-teerz
n. pl. (the border cities or marches of a country)
From Old French frontier, the front or border, from Latin frons, the forehead. The Authorized Version uses the plural once, in the oracle against Moab, of the border cities God would open.

Biblical Definition

Therefore, behold, I will open the side of Moab from the cities, from his cities which are on his frontiers, the glory of the country, Bethjeshimoth, Baalmeon, and Kiriathaim. Moab's border fortresses are called the glory of the country, and they are named one by one before they are opened. The charge against Moab in the previous verse is not military but verbal: because that Moab and Seir do say, Behold, the house of Judah is like unto all the heathen. They had watched their kinsmen fall and drawn the conclusion that Judah's God was nothing special. Ezekiel 25 works through four such neighbours — Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines — and the offence in every case is what they said and felt while Jerusalem burned: Aha, against my sanctuary; thou hast clapped thine hands, and stamped with the feet, and rejoiced in heart with all thy despite. Obadiah brings the same charge against Edom in the sharpest form: thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger. And the refrain that closes each oracle states the purpose of the whole chapter: they shall know that I am the LORD.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): the marches; the border, confine or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country; in Scripture, the border cities of Moab, called the glory of the country.

expand to see more

FRONTIER, n. The marches; the border, confine, or extreme part of a country, bordering on another country.

MARCHES, n. Borders; limits; confines; the frontiers of a country.

DESPITE, n. Extreme malice; violent hatred; malignity; malice irritated or enraged.

BORDER, n. The outer edge of anything; the extremity or exterior limit of a country or region.

VENGEANCE, n. The infliction of pain on another, in return for an injury or offense.

Key Scripture

Eze 25:9 — "Therefore, behold, I will open the side of Moab from the cities, from his cities which are on his frontiers, the glory of the country, Bethjeshimoth, Baalmeon, and Kiriathaim,"

Eze 25:8 — "Thus saith the Lord GOD; Because that Moab and Seir do say, Behold, the house of Judah is like unto all the heathen;"

Eze 25:17 — "And I will execute great vengeance upon them with furious rebukes; and they shall know that I am the LORD, when I shall lay my vengeance upon them."

Oba 1:12 — "But thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother in the day that he became a stranger; neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction; neither shouldest thou have spoken proudly in the day of distress."

Modern Corruption

Malice is assumed harmless while it stays at the level of speech and feeling; Ezekiel's oracles against four nations rest entirely on what those nations said and how they rejoiced at a neighbour's fall.

expand to see more

Nothing in Ezekiel 25 charges Moab, Ammon, Edom, or Philistia with invading Judah. The indictment is a saying, a clapping of hands, a stamping of the feet, and a rejoicing in heart with all thy despite. Secret satisfaction at a rival's ruin is treated as a real offence with real consequences, and the border fortresses called the glory of the country are opened because of it. Proverbs gives the private version of the same warning: rejoice not when thine enemy falleth, and let not thine heart be glad when he stumbleth, lest the LORD see it, and it displease him.

The aggravating factor in Obadiah is kinship. Edom was Esau, brother to Jacob, and the charge is a family charge — thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother, neither shouldest thou have rejoiced over the children of Judah in the day of their destruction. The nearer the relation, the worse the gloating. That has an obvious application within the church, where a man's fall is sometimes received with a satisfaction nobody would say aloud, and where the refrain of the chapter still applies to the watchers as much as to the fallen: they shall know that I am the LORD.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew qatseh (H7097), an end, an extremity, a border; tsebiy (H6643), beauty or glory; naqam (H5360), vengeance.

Hebrew qatseh (H7097) — an extremity, a border, a frontier; his cities which are on his frontiers.

Hebrew tsebiy (H6643) — beauty, glory, honour; the glory of the country.

Hebrew pathach (H6605) — to open, to loosen; I will open the side of Moab.

Hebrew she'at (H7589) — contempt, despite; with all thy despite.

Hebrew naqam (H5360) — vengeance, requital; when I shall lay my vengeance upon them.

Usage

"“his cities which are on his frontiers” — the single occurrence."

"“the house of Judah is like unto all the heathen” — the saying that brought the oracle."

"“thou shouldest not have looked on the day of thy brother” — Obadiah on the same sin."
